subject: physics

moments.title: Franklin's lightning
moments.body: Franklin proposes lightning is electrical and proves it by flying a kite into a thunderstorm — extraordinarily risky; Georg Wilhelm Richmann died attempting a similar experiment in St Petersburg. Franklin introduces the terms 'positive' and 'negative' charge.
moments.takeaway: Lightning is electricity. The terminology Franklin invents is still used.

moments.title: Coulomb's law
moments.body: Coulomb uses a torsion balance to show electric force varies as 1/r^2 — exactly like Newton's gravity. The mathematical similarity hints at deep structure.
moments.takeaway: Electrostatics has the same inverse-square form as gravity.

moments.title: Galvani and Volta
moments.body: Galvani makes frog legs twitch with charged metals; he thinks the muscles store 'animal electricity'. Volta disagrees, showing it is the metals themselves; he builds the first battery (voltaic pile) in 1800.
moments.takeaway: The first source of steady electric current is invented.

moments.title: Millikan's oil drop
moments.body: Millikan measures the charge of the electron by watching charged oil droplets settle in an electric field. e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C. Charge is quantised.
moments.takeaway: The electron's charge is measured directly. Millikan's notebooks were later found to omit some 'bad' data — a permanent ethical controversy.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Coulomb's law and Millikan's measurement underpin all electrostatics. The electron charge is now defined exactly by the 2019 SI redefinition.
now.open_questions: Is the electron truly fundamental, or composite? Are charges precisely quantised by monopoles, or by another mechanism?

reflection: Millikan won a Nobel for the oil-drop experiment, but he selectively excluded data. Was it ethical? How do we evaluate historical scientists by modern standards?
